name: Lean physique looks taller

card.summary: Lower body fat is said to read as taller; attractiveness research exists but nothing on height perception.
card.note: Weight loss carries its own health considerations.

quick.overview:
Proponents say a leaner body looks taller.

Studies of body proportions concern attractiveness, not stature.
quick.mechanism: A narrower silhouette is claimed to emphasise vertical length.
quick.risks: Low as a claim; aggressive dieting has its own health risks. No height-perception studies were found.

lead: The idea that a lean physique makes a person look taller is common in appearance communities. Proponents say that lower body fat gives a longer, narrower silhouette, so the same height reads as taller, and that a lean, defined build also shows off shoulder-to-waist shape.

Perception research gives the idea a basis in one respect: a 2013 set of five experiments by Beck, Emanuele and Savazzi in Psychonomic Bulletin and Review found that taller figures look thinner and that thinner figures also look taller, although the second effect was weaker. The illusion held for rectangles and cylinders and was stronger for photographs and silhouettes of human bodies.[1]

Other body-proportion research concerns attractiveness. A waist-to-chest ratio has been reported as the largest determinant of male attractiveness, so a lean waist with a broader upper body serves two goals at once.[2]

chain: Lower body fat narrows the silhouette
A narrower figure looks taller (height-width illusion)
Same height reads as taller and more athletic
angle.text: People who cut body fat aim for a narrower silhouette that reads as taller and shows muscle definition. In the laboratory, thinner figures were judged taller, with a weaker effect than the reverse illusion in which taller figures look thinner.[1]

paras: The height-width illusion study used drawn and photographed figures rather than real people in a controlled setting, and the authors suggested future work with real bodies.[1]
The waist-hip ratio is used as an indicator of health, and research on attractiveness has examined waist and chest ratios for men.[2]
No studies found on body fat and perceived height in real people. Related laboratory research on the height-width illusion used figures and silhouettes.[1]

timeline.event: Beck, Emanuele and Savazzi report that thinner figures look taller, and taller figures look thinner.[1]

refs.title: A new illusion of height and width: Taller people are perceived as thinner
